question: The book moves forward by questions and answers: what questions do the people and the priests throw back at God in verses 2, 6 and 7?
The verb בָּזָה (bazah, “despise”) is repeated in the chapter: in what concrete way did the priests despise the name of the LORD?
How should we understand “I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated” in the context of peoples and covenants, and what difficulty does this phrase raise for today's reader?
“Present that to your governor”: what have you been offering God that you would not offer to someone you respect?
How does the text describe the covenant with Levi and the way he lived and taught?
The verb בָּגַד (bagad, “act treacherously, be unfaithful”) appears five times: against whom are the people being unfaithful in these verses?
Why does unfaithfulness to “the wife of your youth” make God refuse the offerings on the altar?
“Do we not all have one Father?”: how can this question change the way you treat those close to you?
Whom does God promise to send, and with what two images does the text describe the Lord's coming to the temple?
The word מַלְאָךְ (mal’akh, “messenger”) is the same as in the name Malachi: what messengers appear in verse 1, and how do the Gospels apply this text to John the Baptist?
What complaint do the people make about serving God, and what changes with the “scroll of remembrance” of verse 16?
The text speaks of tithes and of “testing” God: how do you understand the relationship between generosity and trust?
What different fate does the coming day hold for the arrogant and for those who fear the name of the LORD?
The phrase “sun of righteousness” uses the word שֶׁמֶשׁ (shemesh, “sun”): what does the image of a sun that brings healing in its wings suggest?
Why does the last passage of the book bring together Moses and Elijah, and how do the Gospels take up this expectation about Elijah?
The hearts of the fathers turned to the children and those of the children to the fathers: what family reconciliation does this verse stir up in you?
